stories.topic: 1869 — The Year India Was Wired Into the World
stories.summary: In 1869 the Suez Canal opened, collapsing the London-Bombay sea route from a journey around the Cape of Good Hope to a straight shot via Gibraltar and the Red Sea. Around the same time the telegraph arrived (a four-hour London-Bombay delay), the railways spread, and the Companies Act, Contract Act and Evidence Act were imported within a couple of years of being passed in London. The Bombay Stock Exchange opened in 1874, and the American Civil War's interruption of US cotton exports invented an entire Indian cotton trade — grown in Gujarat and Maharashtra, shipped through Bombay to London.
stories.insight: The whole institutional and technological package of the Industrial Revolution was seeded into India almost simultaneously between roughly 1860 and 1913 — India's 'first modernization,' co-extensive with the world's first globalization. Nationalist history has under-recognised this period because conceding it complicates the 'drain' narrative.

stories.topic: The Quinine, the Gin and the Ice from a Frozen Midwest Lake
stories.summary: British India ran on quinine to ward off malaria, but quinine is bitter, so it was dissolved in tonic water and paired with gin — birthing the gin and tonic. To drink the cocktail in Indian heat, you needed ice. There were no fridges. So American entrepreneurs in the Midwest harvested ice from frozen lakes and shipped it across oceans to India. A perfectly absurd, perfectly capitalist solution.
stories.insight: Voluntary global trade routinely solves problems that no central planner could even imagine. A demand in Bombay reaches across the world to a frozen lake in Massachusetts because prices and profit motives stitch together strangers no government bureaucrat ever could.

stories.summary: In the long socialist night, scarcity became so total that families joked about booking a scooter at the birth of a daughter so it would arrive in time for her wedding. Second-hand cars sold for more than new cars because new cars came after years of waiting; second-hand ones existed today. Over 350% import tariffs, a 97.75% top income tax rate, the FERA of 1973, nationalisations of banks/coal/copper/insurance — by the late 1970s it was almost impossible to start a new business or shut a failing one.
stories.insight: When governments throttle voluntary exchange, the absurdities are not bugs but features. The 'scooter at birth' joke is what an economy looks like when you replace prices and freedom with permits and waiting lists — and Amit insists Indira Gandhi's economic regulations did more lasting damage than even the Emergency.

stories.topic: Indira Gandhi Was Embarrassed To Be a Tyrant
stories.summary: Diplomatic-bag leaks from the Emergency period make clear that Indira Gandhi was personally embarrassed about being a third-world dictator and was looking for a face-saving exit. She called the 1977 elections genuinely free and fair — no booth-rigging, no opposition intimidation — because she expected to win. Sanjay Gandhi opposed holding them and wanted her declared. The Indian voter promptly threw her out. As Ajay puts it: it was only Sanjay's mother who could have declared the Emergency, and only Nehru's daughter who could have called the elections.
stories.insight: Even authoritarians crave moral legitimacy, and the Indian electorate is consistently underestimated. India 'lucked out' precisely because Nehru's republican prestige was internalised by his daughter just enough to keep her from going full tyrant. Constitutions live partly in the moral imagination of those who would otherwise break them.

stories.topic: Manmohan Singh, Vijay Kelkar, and a Conference Corridor in Kathmandu
stories.summary: Manmohan Singh ran into Vijay Kelkar in a corridor at a conference in Kathmandu and casually asked, 'So you'll come and work for us, won't you?' Kelkar felt obliged to say yes — and packed his bags for India. He came back without any promise of power, position, or ultimate success, in a period when the Indian project looked likely to crash. The same was true of Manmohan Singh's own return after his PhD in 1962, and of Montek Singh Ahluwalia leaving the World Bank to follow Singh home.
stories.insight: The 1991 reforms didn't appear out of nowhere — they rested on a decade and a half of unglamorous, faith-based work by people who had no expectation that the country would ever reward them. Sharpen the axe even when you'll never cut a tree, because if the moment comes, only the prepared can act.

stories.summary: Recording an episode of The Seen and the Unseen with Kelkar and Ajay Shah at a Carnatic studio, Amit is approached during a break by Kelkar — fresh from the toilet — pointing his finger and saying, 'Amit, I want to give you one piece of advice.' Amit braces for great wisdom from an elder. The advice is left untold here, but Ajay extends it into a creed: don't ask fate to step out of the page of history and shake your hand; sit quietly, dig in, work hard, build knowledge, build community.
stories.insight: Two generations of Indian reformers worked without any guarantee of impact — and that is precisely how impact eventually came. The right ethic is to build knowledge and community, expecting nothing, and to be ready when the world shifts on its axis.

stories.topic: How an Empty Finance Ministry Killed the Reforms
stories.summary: After the 26/11 Mumbai attacks, Manmohan Singh wanted his best man, P. Chidambaram, on the home portfolio. That left finance vacant. Singh planned to hold it himself — until he had to go in for cardiac surgery in January 2009. Sonia Gandhi promoted Pranab Mukherjee in. Mukherjee, an Indira-era socialist, wielded retrospective taxation and other reversals; the economy slid. The same continuity briefly returned under Arun Jaitley around 2014, but politics overtook policy from 2015 onwards.
stories.insight: A single chain of personnel accidents — terror attack, cabinet reshuffle, surgery, replacement minister — undid years of reform momentum. Ajay's deeper lesson: an institutional architecture so dependent on which individuals hold which posts is structurally fragile. Real reform means embedding freedoms into laws and organisational design so the country survives bad ministers.

recommendations.item: Freedom at Midnight
recommendations.creator: Larry Collins and Dominique Lapierre
recommendations.context: The classic narrative history of Indian independence.
recommendations.reason: The book that inspired Ajay's never-written counter-book, Freedom After Midnight — the argument that 1947 delivered political freedom but withheld personal, social and economic freedom, leaving India's freedom struggle structurally incomplete.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: First edition 2019, second edition 2021.
recommendations.reason: A first-principles treatment of state capacity, public administration, law, freedom, market failure and regulation — the very vocabulary Ajay says was missing from the 1991 generation. The book exists because the reformers who saved India in 1991 had not yet built the conceptual toolkit needed to make those reforms institutionally durable.

recommendations.item: The Economic Legacies of Colonial Rule in India
recommendations.creator: Tirthankar Roy
recommendations.context: Essay sent to Ajay by Vinay Sitapati.
recommendations.reason: Argues that colonial-era openness was broadly compatible with Indian interests until the 1920s, and that the nationalist 'drain' framing fundamentally misreads cross-border flows of skill and capital. The price India paid was the price of plugging into a global market — not theft.

recommendations.item: The 1991 Project
recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan / Mercatus Center
recommendations.context: A research and oral-history archive on the 1991 reforms.
recommendations.reason: Chronicles how the 1991 reforms were the result of fifteen years of unglamorous, reward-less intellectual work by Manmohan Singh, Montek Singh Ahluwalia, Vijay Kelkar and others. Antidote to the 'crisis is enough' theory of reform.

recommendations.item: The quest for economic freedom in India
recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: Rajagopalan's magisterial essay on India's slow march to economic freedom.
recommendations.reason: Source of the eye-watering inventory of Indira-era repression that Amit reads aloud — 350%+ tariffs, a 97.75% top income tax rate, FERA, mass nationalisations, 'inflexible labor revenue regulations,' a black economy possibly larger than the formal one.

recommendations.item: Half-Lion: How PV Narasimha Rao Transformed India
recommendations.creator: Vinay Sitapati
recommendations.context: Sitapati's biography of the prime minister of 1991.
recommendations.reason: Sitapati's framing — that 1991 was a re-liberalization, with Nehruvian central planning the real break from a previously open Indian economy — is the spine of Ajay's revisionist account in this episode.

recommendations.item: Jugalbandi: The BJP Before Modi
recommendations.creator: Vinay Sitapati
recommendations.context: Sitapati's history of the BJP before its current incarnation.
recommendations.reason: Recommended alongside Half-Lion as part of Sitapati's larger reading of post-Independence Indian political economy.

recommendations.item: India in the Persianate Age
recommendations.creator: Richard Eaton
recommendations.context: Eaton's reframing of medieval India.
recommendations.reason: Source for the argument that Mughal India's high share of world GDP, and its eventual decline, may have come from how globalising port trade pulled power away from the imperial centre toward the coastal edges. A favourite of the Mughal historians on Amit's longer show.

recommendations.item: Planners vs. Searchers in Foreign Aid
recommendations.creator: William Easterly
recommendations.context: Easterly's 2006-08 ADB paper.
recommendations.reason: Source of the planner-searcher distinction at the heart of this episode. Planners think they know the answers, treat poverty as engineering, impose top-down solutions. Searchers admit ignorance, see poverty as a tangle, use trial-and-error and feedback. Markets and democracies are searchers.

recommendations.item: The Double 'Thank You' Moment
recommendations.creator: John Stossel
recommendations.context: Stossel's short piece on a tiny daily ritual.
recommendations.reason: Buyer says thank you when handing money, seller says thank you when handing the coffee. The 'double thank you' captures the whole moral logic of voluntary exchange — that both sides leave better off, which means trade is positive-sum, not the zero-sum fight our tribal brains expect.

recommendations.item: The End of History?
recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Fukuyama's 1989 essay (note: with a question mark).
recommendations.reason: Read here in its proper sense — not 'history is over' but 'is liberal democracy the telos of history?' Used to mark the post-Berlin-Wall optimism whose lessons a generation born after 1989 has now forgotten.

recommendations.item: How Laissez-Faire Made Sweden Rich
recommendations.creator: Johan Norberg
recommendations.context: Norberg's piece on the actual sequence of Swedish prosperity.
recommendations.reason: Cited against the standard 'look at Scandinavia' rebuttal to free-market arguments. Sweden became rich on free markets first, and only then layered welfare on top — without ever giving up business freedom or ease of doing business.

recommendations.item: Passports Were a Temporary War Measure
recommendations.creator: Speranta Dumitru
recommendations.context: Dumitru's piece on the origin of modern passports.
recommendations.reason: Source of the breathtaking historical fact: before 1914 there were no passports anywhere in the world. The freedom to migrate was treated as an inalienable human right; Versailles tried to restore it; Soviet Russia killed the idea; the EU is the only meaningful modern restoration.

recommendations.item: Pandit's Mind
recommendations.creator: Time magazine (1951)
recommendations.context: 1951 Time cover story on Jawaharlal Nehru.
recommendations.reason: Source of the famous lines that Beatrice and Sidney Webb were 'in a truer sense Nehru's creators than Vishnu and Shiva,' and that Nehru carried 'the aristocratic Brahmin's contempt for the Banya caste' on top of his socialist's contempt for capitalism.

recommendations.item: India's Greatest Civil Servant (Episode 167, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Narayani Basu
recommendations.context: Basu's biography of VP Menon, in conversation.
recommendations.reason: Background to Amit's observation that Patel and Menon performed a 'fast track colonisation of India' in a couple of years that had taken the British two or three centuries — an essential frame for understanding the centralising impulse of 1947.

recommendations.item: India's Founding Moment
recommendations.creator: Madhav Khosla
recommendations.context: Khosla's intellectual history of the Indian Constitution.
recommendations.reason: Source of the framing that the Constitution was a 'pedagogical exercise' as much as a rulebook — written by elites who felt they had to teach a fractious country how to think, and which Amit views with a mix of sympathy and unease.

recommendations.item: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A long conversation on the 1991 reforms.
recommendations.reason: The fuller account of what 1991 achieved — and, painfully, what it left undone in factor markets and agriculture. Amit points listeners there for the deeper version of this episode's chapter on liberalisation.

recommendations.item: The Forgotten Greatness of PV Narasimha Rao (Episode 283, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Sitapati
recommendations.context: Sitapati on Narasimha Rao.
recommendations.reason: The longer conversation on the prime minister who staked all his political capital on 1991 — and on the cadre of reformers who made it possible.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Montek Singh Ahluwalia (Episode 285, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Montek Singh Ahluwalia
recommendations.context: Conversation with one of the architects of 1991.
recommendations.reason: Montek's own account of returning from the World Bank with no promise of power — a first-person source for Ajay's claim that the reforms were built on decades of faith-based work.

recommendations.item: India's Lost Decade (Episode 116, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Puja Mehra
recommendations.context: Conversation around Mehra's book.
recommendations.reason: Background for the claim that India had a golden 1991-2011 and a 'lost decade' afterwards, and that the rot had begun by 2008-09 rather than later.

recommendations.item: The Lost Decade
recommendations.creator: Puja Mehra
recommendations.context: Mehra's book on India's post-2011 economic stall.
recommendations.reason: The book-length argument that Amit and Ajay use as the diagnostic frame for what went wrong after the 1991-2011 golden period.

recommendations.item: Sixteen Stormy Days
recommendations.creator: Tripurdaman Singh
recommendations.context: Singh's history of India's First Constitutional Amendment.
recommendations.reason: Where America's First Amendment protected speech, India's First Amendment damaged it. Nehru clamped down on free speech because he wanted to clamp down on his communist rivals — a great statesman's hubris turning illiberal in real time, captured in the actual Lok Sabha debates.

recommendations.item: The First Assault on Our Constitution (Episode 194, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Tripurdaman Singh
recommendations.context: Long-form companion to Sixteen Stormy Days.
recommendations.reason: The deeper conversation behind the Sixteen Stormy Days recommendation.

recommendations.item: Nehru: The Debates that Defined India
recommendations.creator: Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain
recommendations.context: A collection of Nehru's letters and arguments with Jinnah, Shyama Prasad Mukherjee, Patel, and others.
recommendations.reason: What Amit prizes is not who was right but the manner of the disagreement — these were great minds arguing in good faith, assuming goodwill, an ethic he says has been wholly lost in modern public life. Amit's own cardinal rule of conversation: assume goodwill unless given reason otherwise.

recommendations.item: Nehru's Debates (Episode 262, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain
recommendations.context: Long-form companion to the book.
recommendations.reason: The deeper conversation behind The Debates That Defined India.

recommendations.item: The Clash of Economic Ideas
recommendations.creator: Lawrence H. White
recommendations.context: White's history of twentieth-century economic thought.
recommendations.reason: Linked from the show notes as broader reading on the intellectual currents — Fabian socialism, Soviet planning, Keynesianism, market liberalism — that shaped both Nehru's choices and the world's 1980s about-turn.

recommendations.item: The Art and Science of Economic Policy (Episode 154, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Conversation around the In Service of the Republic.
recommendations.reason: The studio recording around which Amit's bathroom-door anecdote about Vijay Kelkar's parting wisdom takes place.

recommendations.item: Newton the Alchemist. Gandhi the Black Swan (Episode 7, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Earlier EIE episode on Gandhi's intellectual influences.
recommendations.reason: The companion episode that mapped Gandhi's reading; this one performs the same operation on Nehru, locating the Webbs and Harold Laski as his real creators.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's reframing: replace the slippery word 'freedom' with the much sharper word 'consent.' Two questions usually treated as separate — how should I live, and how should the state relate to society — collapse into one answer. Any interaction without consent is coercion; coercion is the ultimate evil. This holds both deontologically (consent is good in itself; without it our lives lose meaning, traceable back to John Locke's right of self-ownership) and consequentially (free societies produce better outcomes for both individuals and the whole). It also exposes the Grand Liberal Paradox: we need a state to protect rights, but the state itself only exists by exacting some of those rights via taxation and the monopoly on violence.

Our brains evolved in tribal scarcity, so we instinctively see gains as theft and wealth as a fixed pie. Angus Maddison's chart of world GDP — flat for millennia, exploding around 1800 with the Industrial Revolution and globalisation — empirically refutes that intuition. Every voluntary transaction makes both parties better off, so more voluntary transactions means more aggregate wealth. Stossel's 'double thank you' moment is the moral signature of this fact: both buyer and seller thank each other.
core_ideas.quote: It's almost as if by magic that the wealth of the world goes up just because of the way you and I exchange things.

core_ideas.explanation: We are wired to assume every beautiful complex thing must have been designed by someone — religion is the archetype of this delusion. But languages, economies, societies, even biological evolution are 'the products of human action, but not of human design' (Adam Ferguson). Economists call it spontaneous order. India's central planners failed not because they lacked intelligence but because the thing they were trying to design only emerges when you let it discover itself.

William Easterly's distinction: a planner thinks he already knows the answers, treats poverty as a technical engineering problem, and imposes solutions from outside. A searcher admits he doesn't know in advance, sees poverty as a tangle of political-social-historical-institutional-technological factors, and works by trial and error with feedback. Markets and democratically accountable politicians are searchers; central planning is the planner mindset writ large. The gulf in outcomes between Indian planning and East Asian searching followed.

Vinay Sitapati's argument, endorsed here: the real break in Indian economic history is not 1991 but 1947. Pre-Independence Bombay and Calcutta were already plugged into the first globalisation; Nehru's Fabian socialism severed those connections. That is why India has fallen out of the world trade story by the time it recovered after WWII (Tirthankar Roy). 1991 was therefore not 'opening up' for the first time but undoing a Nehruvian rupture — which is why it succeeded as quickly as it did.

Ajay's diagnosis of why Indian socialism became more, not less, oppressive even as it visibly failed. The intellectual class — many of them very smart — responded to bad outcomes by doubling down on the ideology that produced them, rather than questioning their priors. Every Hindu rate of growth produced not pragmatism but more controls. 'It's okay to make mistakes; it's not okay to refuse to change course.' This is presented as a permanent warning sign for any ideological community.

core_ideas.concept: Private Sector Confidence as the Engine of Growth
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's insistence that there is only one source of economic growth — the private sector. Growth correlates not with perfect institutions but with the private sector's belief that the state has its act together and that things will incrementally improve. Private actors then commit hours, careers, kids and capital to building firms. The 1979 acceleration came from a small reformist Janata cabinet (Morarji Desai, H.M. Patel, D.T. Lakdawala) signalling a turn; 2011 onwards reversed because the deeds of the state began contradicting its words.

Every country has four elites: political/bureaucratic, business, intellectual, cultural. They need a working social contract. India's 1991-2011 compact was: business invests and builds; when it hits state-shaped landmines, it can file a bug report and find recourse from people who actually understand the problem. The state was not yet fixed, but it was responsive — and that visible responsiveness sustained optimism even amid imperfection. From around 2010 onward the deeds stopped matching the words; new powers, new bad laws and creeping central planning broke the compact and growth decayed.

Why did the United States survive Donald Trump while India keeps being whipsawed by who the home minister is? Because parts of the US state have institutional quality of their own — laws, statutes, organisational designs that hold even when leadership is bad. India's 1991 reformers won policy victories but never enshrined freedoms in durable laws or built the organisational architecture to make them survive a single bad cabinet reshuffle. Real reform means making the country less dependent on which individuals happen to be in which chairs.

core_ideas.concept: The Pre-1914 World of Open Borders
core_ideas.explanation: Before 1914 there were no passports anywhere. People moved freely; royalty wrote 'passports' as letters of personal favour, but the freedom to migrate was treated as inalienable. Capital controls were invented by Adolf Hitler. The Treaty of Versailles tried to restore passport-free travel; international conferences pursued this through the 1960s; Soviet Russia, wanting to imprison its own citizens, vetoed every attempt. Today's only meaningful restoration of the old freedom is the European Union. We have normalised an unfreedom that would have been unrecognisable to our great-grandparents.

Two periods (1927-47 and 1962-77) when the Indian situation looked irrecoverable, and when many gave up or left. The best and brightest dug in — wrote longhand letters, debated rival visions of India, built knowledge and built each other — without any promise of reward, power or even success. When the moment came in 1947 and 1991, the documents and the people existed. The right ethic in dark times is to do the unrewarded preparatory work, because the only way to be ready when the world turns is to have done the work nobody asked you to do.
core_ideas.quote: Do not ask fate to step out of the page of history and shake your hand.

core_ideas.explanation: We mistake the long arc of progress for an automatic mechanism. It isn't. Weimar Germany's flourishing turned into Nazi Germany. Deng Xiaoping's 1978 dawn turned into today's surveillance China. Yeltsin-era Russia turned into Putin's Russia. The reverse case — post-war Germany and Japan rebuilt as functioning democracies — is also instructive: culture is not destiny. But the lesson cuts both ways. Freedom must be actively defended, and any community that takes it as given will lose it.

core_ideas.concept: Why Scandinavia Doesn't Refute the Argument
core_ideas.explanation: The standard rebuttal to 'freedom drives prosperity' points at Scandinavian welfare states. Two answers. (a) Scandinavia retains very high economic freedom — easy to start a business, do business, live your life. (b) These countries became rich first under genuinely free markets; only after reaching a high standard of living did they layer welfare on top. The sequence matters: welfare did not produce their wealth, freedom did, and welfare is what wealth allows you to afford.

Ajay's elegant line: it was only Sanjay Gandhi's mother who could have declared the Emergency, and only Jawaharlal Nehru's daughter who could have called the elections. Indira Gandhi's republican upbringing left enough moral residue that she was personally embarrassed about being a third-world tyrant — she wanted out, called genuinely free elections, and the voter promptly evicted her. India 'lucked out,' and the luck lived inside her conscience.

core_ideas.concept: Nehru's Real Creators Were the Webbs and Laski
core_ideas.explanation: Time magazine's 1951 cover story put it brutally: Beatrice and Sidney Webb, the godparents of Fabian socialism, were 'in a truer sense Nehru's creators than Vishnu and Shiva.' Layered on top was 'the aristocratic Brahmin's contempt for the Banya caste,' fused with the British socialist's contempt for capitalism. Harold Laski, John Kenneth Galbraith said, was the 'centre of his thinking' — an unnamed wit observed that at every cabinet meeting an empty chair was kept for Laski. Nehru's policy errors were not personal flaws so much as the faithful execution of a wrong intellectual tradition imported wholesale.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's opening: there's a young cat mewing in the background, and he must clarify that 'it sounds like the wailing of all the dispossessed and the hungry and the starving through these many, many years of India's tormented journey.'
Amit on his own unwritten book: he proposed Freedom After Midnight to the New India Foundation around 2008, never wrote it because 'I'm a lazy bum,' and the foundation rejected the proposal anyway.

The pre-1991 scarcity joke: 'When a girl child is born, book a scooter so it arrives by the time she gets married.' India was the one country where a second-hand car cost more than a new one — because a new one took years and a used one was already there.

Amit on Indira Gandhi's economic legacy: people remember the Emergency as her worst excess, but 'her economic regulations were far worse — they kept millions of people in India in poverty for decades longer than necessary.'

P. Chidambaram's pithy summary of the era: India 'suspected capitalists, it suspected the profit motive, and it tried to nail it down, block it, and thought that all growth would come from government planning.'
Ajay on the failure mode of Indian central planners: every shortfall was met by intensification — 'the floggings will continue until the morale improves.'
Ajay on Indira's rare moment of restraint: 'Only Sanjay Gandhi's mother could have declared the Emergency. And only Jawaharlal Nehru's daughter could have declared elections.'

Amit on the flow of episodes where they 'agree to disagree': viewers sometimes scratch their heads wondering 'do you guys agree on this or not?' — followed by Amit fining Ajay double recommendations next week for not bringing any this time.
Nehru to J.R.D. Tata: 'Do not speak to me of profit. It is a dirty word.' Used as the canonical line for Nehruvian distrust of capitalism.

The 1951 Time magazine line: Beatrice and Sidney Webb were 'in a truer sense' Nehru's creators 'than Vishnu and Shiva.' Time also coined the contempt-stack: socialist contempt for capitalism plus aristocratic-Brahmin contempt for the Banya caste, producing his attacks on the 'Banya civilization' and 'wealth's cutthroat civilization.'
Ram Guha's anonymous wit on Nehru's cabinet: at every cabinet meeting there was an empty seat — and Harold Laski sat on it.

Abraham Lincoln: 'If I have six hours to cut a tree, I'll spend the first five sharpening the axe.' Used as the moral of how the 1991 reforms were really decades of preparatory work cashed in at the right moment.
Adam Ferguson's eighteenth-century formulation of spontaneous order: 'the products of human action, but not of human design.'
Francis Fukuyama's End of History — invoked with the original question mark: not 'history is over' but 'is liberal democracy the telos of history?'

Ajay's parting brag-correction on European integration: people now move freely between France, Germany, Belgium and the UK without passports. 'Oh, scratch that — not UK.' (A wry acknowledgement of Brexit.)
